title: STARTbeforeCORT randomized controlled multicenter trial - STArt Respiratory sTabilization BEFORE umbilical CORd Transfusion (SBC) in extremely preterm infants - a randomized controlled multicentre trial of safety and efficiency
summary:
Background: Delayed cord clamping may be beneficial for preterm infants, as it reduces the risk of mortality and severe morbidity compared to immediate cord clamping after birth. However, preterm infants often require immediate respiratory support. With the new STARTbeforeCORT (SBC) approach, the infant is therefore immediately handed over to the neonatal team with the umbilical cord and placenta still intact. Respiratory support begins immediately, while the elevated placenta allows blood to flow by gravity and be transfused from the placenta over a prolonged period.

Research Question: Does the incidence of severe acute complications of extreme preterm birth (22+0 to 27+6 weeks of gestation) differ between delayed cord clamping (DCC) and SBC? With SBC, respiratory stabilization can begin immediately after birth rather than only after DCC is completed; therefore, it must be determined whether SBC offers advantages.

Methodology: This is a randomized, controlled, multicenter study involving 236 infants. A randomization procedure prior to birth determines whether DCC (clamping the umbilical cord after 30–60 seconds) or SBC (immediate care with the umbilical cord intact, clamping no later than ten minutes) is performed. There are no deviations from routine cardiac and respiratory monitoring or standard care. Only cesarean section births are included in the study.

interventions.name: Intervention (SBC): The preterm infant, with the umbilical cord and placenta intact, is immediately handed over to the neonatal team. Respiratory stabilization begins immediately, even before the umbilical cord is clamped. At the same time, placental blood flows into the infant by gravity.
Control: delayed cord clamping (DCC) before start of postnatal stabilization measures

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
informed parental consent or consent of the legal guardian
Exclusion criteria:
• spontaneous delivery
• Emergency delivery in women admitted on an emergency basis, where immediate delivery is required and there is insufficient time for counselling and obtaining written informed consent before birth.
• non-last infant in multiple pregnancies as SBC is only feasible in the last multiple
• severe congenital anomalies affecting breathing control (cerebral anomalies, chromosomal anomalies, prenatally diagnosed intracranial hemorrhage, etc.)
or gas exchange (pulmonary hypoplasia due to congenital diaphragmatic hernia or oligo/anhydramnion present at <22 weeks gestational age or other pulmonary or intrathoracic malformations, etc.)
or hemodynamics (cyanotic heart disease, ductal dependent systemic perfusion, or similar)
• decision not to provide full life support / decision for palliative care only before study entry
• parents not able to understand the study due to language problems
